title: The Bride Wants the Groom to Lead
author: J. Chase Davis
summary: In this sermon transcript opening a series on Song of Solomon, the pastor argues the biblical love poem should be read on two simultaneous levels: as a literal, unembarrassed account of marital courtship and desire, and as an allegory of Christ's relationship to the church, rejecting the two extremes of either spiritualizing the text away from its erotic content or reducing it to a purely secular dating-advice series. Working through the first chapter verse by verse, he builds his central argument around the bride's opening desire that the groom 'draw me after you; let us run' -- reading this as evidence that a wife's healthy desire is for her husband's leadership, which he distinguishes sharply from wanting to simply be agreed with. He frames the bride's admiration of the groom as rooted in reputation and respect while the groom's attraction is rooted in her physical beauty, presenting this asymmetry as a normal and biblically affirmed pattern of male-female attraction rather than something to correct. The sermon closes by extending the marital picture allegorically: the church as bride desires Christ's leadership and intimacy the same way the bride in the text desires her groom's, with marriage itself functioning as a real institution that also points toward that greater spiritual reality.
points: The sermon's central interpretive move is treating the bride's line 'draw me after you; let us run' as the text's own argument that a wife's desire for her husband's leadership is native to healthy marital love, not an imposed patriarchal expectation.

It draws a sharp distinction between wanting to be led and wanting to be agreed with, arguing that a wife who only accepts leadership 'in the way she feels like being led, when she's in the mood' is not actually describing leadership at all.

The sermon deliberately refuses to choose between the two traditional interpretive camps (pure Christ-and-church allegory vs. pure dating-and-marriage guide), arguing both readings are licensed by the text and mutually reinforcing.

The asymmetry it identifies -- her desire rooted in his reputation and respect, his attraction rooted in her physical beauty -- is presented as a normal, textually-supported pattern of attraction rather than a problem requiring correction.
quotes: This is, of course, contrary to many feminist dating ideals where the idea is that the man and woman are interchangeable. Instead, she longs for him to provide leadership, and she is honest about what she wants.
The bride wants the groom to lead. This speaks to wives and women more generally too. A good wife is ready for her husband to lead. This is what many wives want to experience.

The challenge many wives experience today is that they want to be led, but only in the way they feel like being led, when they're in the mood to be led. And really, what you're saying when you say that is that you basically want to be agreed with.
We have the woman's admiration and desire of the man, and that is rooted in his name, his reputation, and the respect he has in the community. Her love is born out of admiration and respect.
Biblically, and even from creation, we see that marriage is a holy union. This union between a man and a woman, where the two will become one flesh, is fundamental to the fabric of creation.
We seek his face. We long for deeper intimacy with Christ. And what does Christ do in this situation?
